views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Answer the already-signed Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs with a calibrated, WTO-framed retaliation on politically sensitive U.S. exports (continue and, if needed, expand the sorghum anti-dumping track; prepare a short, targeted agricultural list) while keeping a live channel for talks on the still-unannounced Section 301 package. Do not concede Made in China 2025 / tech-transfer architecture, and do not launch a broad pre-emptive tariff war before USTR actually publishes findings and remedies. The aim is deterrence and domestic credibility after the Liu He snub, not a race to the bottom.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not yet high. The live U.S. measures as of 21 March are Section 201 solar/washer safeguards (22 Jan) and global Section 232 metals tariffs signed 8 March; China is a small direct steel supplier (~2% of U.S. steel imports), so the realized export hit is limited. The larger danger is prospective: a 300-page Section 301 report and shock-value tariff/investment package aimed at IP, forced tech transfer, and industrial policy is expected imminently (Politico, 21 Mar; Trump 7 Mar tweet; Covington 15 Mar). That targets the development model, not just metals. Macro data do not yet show a bite: industrial production still ~6% y/y, reserves ~$3.16tn and stable, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY stronger (~6.32 vs ~6.62 six months earlier), so this is not FX stress or export-hub unemployment. Action should therefore be a measured mirror of 232, not maximal escalation and not concession. Beijing has already vowed “necessary measures” and opened a sorghum AD probe after the January safeguards; U.S. soy (~$12bn) is the obvious larger lever and is already spooking the farm belt, but a full soy cutoff would also raise Chinese feed/pork costs. Unilateral U.S. 232 and “trade wars are good, and easy to win” have irritated third parties, so China can retaliate proportionally, file at the WTO, and still invite negotiation on 301 without pre-paying structural reform.
key_factors: Section 301 findings and remedies are imminent but not yet published; the live fight is still 201/232
232 metals tariffs are signed but China’s direct steel/aluminum exposure is small
China macro still healthy: IP ~+6% y/y, reserves stable, CNY firmer — dispute not biting the real economy
U.S. farm-belt (sorghum already probed; soy the larger lever) is the highest-leverage, lowest-self-harm retaliation channel if kept calibrated
Liu He talks were undercut by the 232 announcement; some visible response is needed for credibility without locking in a larger 301 package
U.S. unilateralism and ally irritation create space to frame China as defending multilateral rules

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit).
Trump announces plan to impose 25% tariff on steel and 10% on aluminum imports (Section 232). Global scope; China is a smaller direct supplier share than some other exporters.
Trump tweets: "trade wars are good, and easy to win."
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
China industrial production still ~106.0 (same period previous year = 100) as of 2018-03; growth intact, not a recessionary export shock.
China total reserves ex-gold ~$3.16tn in March 2018, slightly higher over the window — no reserve-drain / financial-stability stress.
CNY/USD ~6.32 on 21 Mar 2018 versus ~6.62 in late Sep 2017 (yuan stronger, not under tariff-driven depreciation pressure).
Expected ~300-page Section 301 report with recommendations; tariff action described as geared more toward shock value and leverage than methodical engagement.
More worrying to China are separate Section 301 sanctions; hundreds of Chinese companies could be singled out.
China is only a little more than 2% of U.S. steel imports; Beijing’s initial 232 reaction was cautious and still hoped to keep talking.
MOFCOM “resolutely opposed” 232 and said China will assess damage and firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.
China already launched a sorghum AD probe after January safeguards; soybeans (over half of U.S. soy exports) are the widely discussed next lever.
After 232, U.S. is poised to implement 301 sanctions on China IP; Beijing has signaled it is prepared to respond, including via politically sensitive tariffs and WTO challenge.
